While I, eager to serve, am always here like a son, it is not fitting for you, gods on earth, to resort to another hermitage.
brahmapuran:74:49	This hermitage is holy for all — that is my view. Enough of going to another hermitage, O sages.
Hearing the sage's words and remembering his task of creating obstacles, the lord of the Ganas, with joined palms, spoke to the brahmins:

Are we bought with food? Why does Gautama restrain us? We cannot go to our own dwellings by conciliation.
brahmapuran:74:52	This excellent brahmin, our benefactor, does not deserve punishment. Therefore I will decide by wit; let all agree to it.
Then all the best of brahmins said, "Let it be done; for his benefit and wishing the good of the worlds,
do whatever would be for the good of all brahmins." Hearing the brahmins' words, the lord of the Ganas accepted their word:
What is done will be of virtue, especially for Gautama.

Having gained the consent of all the brahmins again and again, the noble-minded one himself became a brahmin and bowed again to the brahmins; abiding by his mother's wish, the wise lord of the Ganas said to Jaya:

Act so that no one else knows, O fair-faced one. Taking the form of a cow, go where Gautama is.
brahmapuran:74:58	Eat and destroy the rice, and behave strangely, O lovely one. When struck, or at a 'hum' or even a glance, fall down with a pitiful cry, neither dying nor living.
Vijaya did so, abiding by the will of the lord of obstacles; where the brahmin Gautama was, Jaya, in the form of a cow,
went, eating the rice. Gautama saw her; seeing the strange cow, the brahmin warded her off with a blade of grass.
Being warded off by him, the cow cried out and fell; when she fell, a great cry of dismay arose.
Hearing the cry and seeing Gautama's action, the distressed brahmins, led by the king of obstacles, said:
We are all leaving here; we should not stay in your hermitage. We were all nourished like sons; we take leave of you, O bull among sages.
Hearing the words of the departing brahmins, the sage was as if struck by a thunderbolt and fell before the brahmins.
All the brahmins said to him: "See this one fallen on the ground, the goddess, mother of the Rudras, purifier of the worlds, beloved.
Now that this cow, the embodiment of the gods of the holy places, has fallen by the force of fate, O best of sages, it remains for us to go.
The vows we practised would perish by staying in your hermitage; we have no other wealth, O Brahman, but austerity alone."
Standing before the brahmins, Gautama humbly said:
You alone are my refuge; you should make me pure.
Then the Lord, the king of obstacles, surrounded by the brahmins, spoke:
She neither dies there nor lives; what shall we say, in this doubtful case, about expiation or its course?
How will this cow rise, and what is the expiation for this? Please tell me all that; I will do it without doubt.
This wise one will speak with the agreement of all; his word will be our authority for you, Gautama.
Urged by the brahmins and by the mighty Gautama, the creator of obstacles in a brahmin's form spoke these words to all:

With the agreement of all I will speak truthfully; let the sages and Gautama too assent to my words.
brahmapuran:74:76	We have heard that in the matted locks of Maheshvara stays the water that was in the water-pot of Brahma, born of the unmanifest.
brahmapuran:74:77	Bring it quickly through austerity and discipline, and with it sprinkle this cow lying on the ground, O Lord; then we shall all dwell in your house as before.
When the best of brahmins had said this in the assembly of brahmins, a shower of flowers fell there and cries of victory rose. Then Gautama, bowing with joined palms, spoke:
By austerity, by the grace of fire, by the grace of gods and Brahman, and by your grace, may my resolve be accomplished.
So be it, said the brahmins; taking leave of that bull among sages, they went to their own places, rich in food and water.
When those brahmins had gone, the lord of the Ganas, with his brother and Jaya, well pleased and his purpose achieved, returned.
When the groups of brahmins had gone, and Ganesha too, Gautama, the best of sages, his impurity destroyed by austerity,
meditated on the matter: "What is this that has happened to me?" Meditating thus many times, the sage came to know through wisdom, O brahmin.
He understood it as for the purpose of the gods, the course of his own fault, the benefit of the worlds and the pleasing of Shambhu,
the pleasing of Uma and the bringing of the Ganga: "I consider everything conducive to good, and there is no fault in me."
Reflecting thus in his mind, the best of brahmins became well pleased: "Having worshipped the three-eyed, bull-bannered lord of the worlds,
I will bring the best of rivers; may Girija be pleased with me, the co-wife of the Mother of the world who dwells in Maheshvara's matted locks."
Having resolved thus, that foremost of sages, Gautama, went from Brahmagiri to Kailasa, ruled by the fierce-bowed god, worshipped by the gods with his beloved and the hosts of brahmins.
Having observed the Shrutis and Hara's lordship over the universe by all means of knowledge, people perform their dharmas and enjoy pleasures; this is the glory of Sadashiva.

Whatever is to be accomplished — most excellent and dear — through the effects, actions, agents and means taught in the Veda and in the world, that is declared the perfection of the beginningless maker.

Having meditated on the excellent supreme Brahman, the chief, which is the essence and is to be worshipped, attaining which the liberated are not born again — the liberation of true yogins is that husband of Uma.
As Shambhu of immeasurable maya takes forms for the good of the world, so you take forms fit for union with them; thus, O Mother, is fidelity to one's husband in you.
As he praised thus, the bull-bannered god appeared before him, glorious, with Uma, surrounded by Ganesha and the other hosts.
Shambhu came in person and, pleased, spoke to him:
What shall I give you, Gautama? I am pleased by your auspicious devotion, hymn and vows; ask for something even the gods find hard to obtain.
Hearing the words of the one whose form is the world, Gautama, skilled in speech, his body covered with tears of joy, reflected:
Ah, fate! Ah, dharma! Ah, the worship of brahmins! Ah, how strange the ways of the world! Ah, Creator, salutation to you!
Give me the auspicious Ganga who dwells in your locks, O one worshipped by the gods, if you are pleased, O lord of gods; salutation to you, abode of the three Vedas.
You have asked for the benefit of the three worlds; now ask without fear for your own benefit.
May the devotees who praise you and the Goddess with this hymn be rich in all desires — this I choose.
So be it, said the lord of gods, well pleased; "ask other boons of me too, free from anxiety."
Thus addressed, Gautama joyfully said to Shankara:

Release this goddess dwelling in your locks, purifying, purifier of the world, your beloved, O lord of the world, on Brahma's mountain.
brahmapuran:75:36	May she be the holy place of all, as far as she goes to the ocean; may all sins such as brahmin-slaying, of mind, speech and body,
brahmapuran:75:37	be dissolved by merely bathing in her, O Shankara. Whatever fruit there is at eclipses of moon and sun, at the solstices and equinoxes,
brahmapuran:75:38	at the solar transits, at vaidhriti, and at other holy places — may that merit arise from merely remembering her, O Hara.
brahmapuran:75:39	Austerity is declared praiseworthy in the Krita age, the work of sacrifice in the Treta, sacrifice and gift in the Dvapara, and gift alone in the Kali age.
brahmapuran:75:40	The dharmas of the ages and the dharmas of lands, whatever dharma is commended where according to place and time,
brahmapuran:75:41	whatever merit is gained elsewhere through bathing, giving and restraint — may that merit arise from merely remembering her, O Hara.
brahmapuran:75:42	Wherever she goes, as far as she flows to the sea, there you should be present — let this be the excellent boon.
brahmapuran:75:43	For ten yojanas beyond by count, even great sinners who enter within that area,
brahmapuran:75:44	and their ancestors, and those coming to bathe, O Shiva, and those who die while bathing or in between, may they partake of liberation.
brahmapuran:75:45	On one side all the holy places in heaven, the mortal world and Rasatala; this one is superior to them. Enough, Shambhu; salutation to you.
Hearing Gautama's words, Shiva said, "So be it; there has not been and will not be a holy place higher than this.
True, true, again true, and established in the Veda: the Gautami is the holiest of all." Having said this, he vanished.
When the Lord worshipped by the world had gone, Gautama, full of strength by his command, taking the lock with that best of rivers, entered Brahmagiri surrounded by the gods.
When Gautama arrived with the lock, O Narada, a shower of flowers fell there and the lords of the gods assembled,
and the illustrious sages, brahmins and kshatriyas, joyfully honouring that brahmin with cries of victory.
Hearing Gautama's words, the Ganga accepted what the brahmin said and divided herself into three, in heaven, the mortal world and Rasatala.
In heaven she went in four streams, in the mortal world in seven, in Rasatala in four; thus she has fifteen forms.
Everywhere she is all beings, destroyer of all sins, ever granting all desires; she alone is sung in the Veda.
Mortals see only the one gone to the mortal world, not the one gone below; nor do mortals of ignorant mind see the one gone to heaven.
As far as the goddess goes to the ocean, so far she is remembered as full of the gods; released by Gautama, she went toward the eastern ocean.
Then Gautama, tiger among sages, circumambulated the auspicious mother of the world, frequented by gods and sages.
Having first worshipped the three-eyed lord of the gods, Gautama resolved, "I will bathe on both banks."
As soon as he was remembered, the ocean of compassion appeared there; Gautama asked Sharva how the bathing there should be accomplished,
with joined palms, bowed in devotion to the three-eyed god:
O god of gods, great lord, tell me properly the procedure for bathing at the holy place, for the good of the worlds.

O great sage, hear the whole procedure concerning the Godavari. First perform the Nandimukha rite and purify the body,
brahmapuran:76:19	feed brahmins and take their leave; they go observing celibacy, avoiding talk with the fallen.
brahmapuran:76:20	He whose hands, feet and mind are well restrained, who has learning, austerity and fame, enjoys the fruit of the holy place.
brahmapuran:76:21	Abandoning impurity of feeling, established in his own dharma, relieving the weary, he should give food as fitting.
brahmapuran:76:22	He should give garments and blankets to the needy and the good, listening to the divine stories of Hari and those arising from the Ganga; going by this procedure, one properly obtains the fruit of the holy place.
He had no offspring, and so he became anxious; having summoned Vasishtha to his house and duly worshipped him,
the king spoke about the cause of offspring. Hearing these words, he meditated and said to the king:
O king, with your wife, always be devoted to the worship of sages.
Having said this, the sage went to his own place, O brahmin. One day a treasury of austerity came to the house of that royal sage.
He worshipped that sage, and the sage, pleased, said, "Name a boon, O illustrious one." When this was said, he chose sons.
The sage said to the king: "From one wife let there be a son who continues the line, and from the other sixty thousand sons."
When the sage had given the boon and gone, thousands of sons were born. He performed very many sacrifices, horse sacrifices with good fees.
In one horse sacrifice, duly consecrated, the king appointed his sons with armies to guard the horse.
Finding an opportunity somewhere, Shatakratu stole the horse; searching, those sons did not see the horse then.
Sixty thousand of them, skilled in various kinds of fighting — while Sagara's sons looked on, the Rakshasas
took that consecrated horse and went to Rasatala; the sons of Sagara did not see the Rakshasas, who were possessed of illusion.
Not seeing the horse, the sons of mighty Sagara wandered here and there and still did not see the horse.
Then they went to the world of the gods, searching mountains, lakes and forests, and did not see the horse.
The king, for whom blessings had been recited and auspicious rites performed by the priests, not seeing the lovely animal, fell into anxiety.
Wandering, all the sons of Sagara came to the world of the gods, searching for the horse, but the horse was not there either.
Then they came to the earth, the mountains and forests; there too the princes did not see the horse.
Meanwhile a divine voice arose there: "The horse is tied in Rasatala and nowhere else, O sons of Sagara."
Hearing those words and wishing to go to Rasatala, the sons of Sagara dug up the whole earth all around.
Tormented by hunger, eating dry earth day and night, they dug and quickly went to Rasatala.
Hearing that those mighty, skilful sons of the king had come, the Rakshasas, terrified, went near Kapila.
The very wise Kapila lay there in Rasatala; formerly he had accomplished an excellent task for the gods.
Weary from sleeplessness when the task had been accomplished, the glorious Kapila said to the gods, "Give me a place to sleep."
They gave him Rasatala; the sage said again to the gods, "Whatever fool wakes me will quickly become ashes.
Then I will lie below; otherwise there is no sleep." The hosts of gods said, "So be it," and he lies in Rasatala.
Knowing his power, the Rakshasas, possessed of illusion, devised a means to kill all the sons of Sagara.
Afraid of fighting, the Rakshasas quickly came to where that very irascible sage Kapila was,
and hastily tying the horse near his head, stood far off in silence, watching to see what would happen.
Then all the sons of Sagara, entering Rasatala, saw the horse tied and the man lying there.
They considered him the thief and destroyer of the sacrifice: "Let us kill this great sinner and take the horse to the king."
Some said, "Let us take the tethered animal; what use is he?" Other heroes said, "We are kings and rulers;
let us wake this great sinner and kill him with kshatriya valour." They struck the sage with their feet, speaking harsh words.
Then Kapila, best of sages, in great anger looked at the sons of Sagara and in his anger reduced them to ashes.
All the sons of Sagara were burned there; but King Sagara, being consecrated, knew nothing of it.
Narada told the great-souled Sagara where Kapila was and where the horse was,
the trick of the Rakshasas and the destruction of the sons of Sagara. Then the king, filled with anxiety, did not know what to do.
He had another son, known as Asamanjas; out of folly he threw children and citizens into the water.
Then Sagara was informed by the assembled citizens; knowing his misconduct, the king became angry and said
to his ministers: "Let him leave the country — this Asamanjas who has abandoned kshatriya dharma and kills children."
Hearing Sagara's words, the ministers quickly expelled the king's son; Asamanjas went to the forest.
The sons of Sagara have all perished in Rasatala by a brahmin's curse, and the one has gone to the forest; now what is my course?
The son of Asamanjas was known as Amshuman; the king had the boy brought and told him the task.
Having propitiated Kapila, the boy Amshuman gave the horse to Sagara, and then the sacrifice was completed.
His son was the radiant and righteous Dilipa; his son was known as the wise Bhagiratha.
Hearing of the fate of all his grandfathers, greatly grieved, he humbly asked Sagara, tiger among kings:
How can there be deliverance for all the sons of Sagara? The king said to Bhagiratha, "Kapila knows, my son."
Hearing his words, the boy went to Rasatala, bowed to Kapila and told him everything.
The sage meditated long and said, "Having propitiated Shankara with austerity, flood your ancestors with the water of his locks, O best of kings;
then you and your ancestors will be fulfilled." Saying "I will do so," he bowed to the sage and said again:
Where should I go, best of sages, and what must I do? Tell me that.
Go to Kailasa, best of men, and praise Maheshvara; practise austerity as you are able, and then you will obtain what you desire.
Hearing the sage's words, he bowed to him and went to the mountain Kailasa; becoming pure, the boy, with a boy's ways, resolved on austerity, and Bhagiratha said:

I am a child with a child's mind, O Lord who bears the young moon; I know nothing; therefore be pleased, O Lord.
brahmapuran:78:57	To those who, devoted to my good, sometimes help me by words, thoughts and deeds — for their good, O lord of the immortals, I bow here to Soma, worshipped by the gods and others.
brahmapuran:78:58	May Shiva fulfil the wishes of those by whom I was begotten and raised, of the same lineage and the same dharma; I ever bow to the one crowned with the young moon.
As he spoke thus, Shiva appeared before him and, offering a boon, said to Bhagiratha:
What cannot be accomplished by the hosts of gods I will surely give you; speak without fear, O wise Bhagiratha.
Bhagiratha, bowing to the Lord, joyfully said to Shankara:
Give me the best of rivers who dwells in your locks, to purify my ancestors, O lord of gods; then all will be attained.
Maheshvara laughed and said to Bhagiratha:
She is given to you by me, my son; now praise her, O one of good vows.
Hearing the god's words, for that purpose he performed great austerity and praised the Ganga with devotion and a disciplined mind.
Obtaining her grace too, the boy, not like a boy, took the Ganga received from Maheshvara and went to Rasatala.
He told the great-souled sage Kapila, and having carefully established the Ganga in the manner described,
he circumambulated and, with joined palms, said:
O Goddess, my ancestors, through the curse of the great sage Kapila, have gone to a bad fate, Mother; therefore you should save them.
Saying "So be it," the river of the gods, benefactor of all, for the benefit of the worlds and to purify the ancestors,
and especially to fill the ocean drunk by Agastya, the river of the gods, who destroys sins by mere remembrance,
did as Bhagiratha asked: the princes, sons of Sagara, lying burned to ashes at the bottom of Rasatala,
she flooded, and then filled up the excavation. Then, having flooded Meru, as she stood there, the boy king said:
You must be in the land of action. Saying "So be it," she came to the Himalaya; from the holy Himalaya mountain she came to the land of Bharata.
Through its midst the holy river went toward the eastern ocean. Thus this Ganga too has been told to you, the kshatriya one, O great sage.
She is of Maheshvara, of Vishnu and of Brahma, and purifying; the Bhagirathi, the river of the gods, resting on the peaks of the Himalaya.
Thus the water of Maheshvara's locks became twofold: south of the Vindhya the Ganga is called the Gautami; north of the Vindhya she is called the Bhagirathi.
Then the sinner, exhausted, could not make out water, land, pit, path or directions, nor any refuge.
Where shall I go? Where shall I stay? What shall I do? he thought. "I take the lives of all living beings, like Death.
Now a hailstorm has come, a thing that brings my end. I see no protector, no rock or tree nearby."
Thinking thus in many ways, the hunter saw near him in the forest a tree, like the lord of trees, as the moon is among stars,
as the lion among beasts, the householder among the stages of life, the mind among the senses — a tree, protector of creatures,
an excellent, bright tree adorned with branches and shoots. Taking shelter under it, the hunter sat down in wet clothes,
remembering his wife and children — whether they lived or not. Meanwhile the sun set there.
On that same tree a pigeon lived with his wife, surrounded by sons and grandsons, in that excellent tree,
happy and fearless, well satisfied and content; many years had passed as that bird dwelt there.
His wife was devoted to him, and he well pleased with her; in a hollow of that excellent tree, free from water, wind and fire,
the pigeon always stayed, surrounded by wife and sons. That day, by the force of fate, the pigeon and his mate
both went for food; the pigeon returned to the tree, but she, by fate, my son, remained in a cage,
caught by the hunter, still alive. The pigeon, seeing the children without their mother,
the terrible rain having come and the sun having set, and seeing his hollow without her, lamented.
The king of pigeons did not know she was bound in a cage; the pigeon began to praise the virtues of his beloved:

Even now she has not come, the auspicious one who increases my joy, the mother of my dharma, the mistress of my body,
brahmapuran:80:31	ever my helper in dharma, wealth, desire and liberation, smiling when I am pleased and wiping away my sorrow when I am angry,
brahmapuran:80:32	my friend in counsel, ever devoted to my words — even now the auspicious one has not come, though the sun has set.
brahmapuran:80:33	She knows no vow, mantra, deity, dharma or wealth other than her husband — devoted to her husband, whose life is her husband, whose counsel is her husband, who loves her husband —
brahmapuran:80:34	even now the auspicious one has not come. What shall I do, where shall I go? What is my house or forest to me? Without her they look empty.
brahmapuran:80:35	With her it is joined with fortune, whether fearsome or fair. Even now my beloved has not come, by whom the house is called a house.
brahmapuran:80:36	Without her I will not live; I will give up my dear body. What will the children do? And I, again, have lost my dharma.
Hearing her husband lamenting thus, she, still in the cage, spoke these words to her husband:

I am here, bound and helpless, O best of birds; I have been brought by the hunter and bound with nooses, O wise one.
brahmapuran:80:39	I am blessed and favoured that my husband speaks of my virtues, whether present or not; I am fulfilled, without doubt.
brahmapuran:80:40	When the husband is pleased, all the deities are pleased with women; in the opposite case women surely meet destruction.
brahmapuran:80:41	You are my god, my lord, my friend, my refuge; you are my vow, the supreme Brahman, heaven and liberation.
brahmapuran:80:43	Do not grieve, auspicious one; make your mind firm in dharma. By your grace I have enjoyed various pleasures. Enough of grief; do not sink; make your mind firm in dharma.
Hearing his beloved's words, he quickly came down from the excellent tree to where the pigeon hen was in the cage.
Coming to her, seeing his beloved and the hunter lying as if dead, he said to her, "I will free you; the hunter is now motionless."

What you have said befits us both, and you think rightly; but there is something to be said too — hear it, fair-faced one.
brahmapuran:80:57	Someone supports a thousand, another a hundred, another ten, another himself in comfort; we fill our bellies with difficulty.
brahmapuran:80:58	Some have wealth of grain in pits, others wealth in granaries, some wealth stored in jars; our wealth is what we carry in our beaks.
brahmapuran:80:59	How can I honour this weary guest, dear one?
Fire, water, kind words, and whatever grass and wood there is — these too should be given to one in need; and this hunter is tormented by cold.
Hearing his beloved's words, the king of birds climbed the tree and looked about; then he saw a fire far away.
Going to the place of the fire, he brought a firebrand in his beak, and the pigeon lit a fire before the hunter.
Again and again that king of pigeons threw dry wood, leaves and grass into the fire at midnight.
Seeing the fire blazing, the hunter, suffering from cold, warmed his numbed limbs and found comfort.
Seeing the hunter burning with the fire of hunger, the pigeon hen said to her husband, "Do not free me, illustrious one;
I will satisfy the suffering hunter with my own body; may you attain the worlds of those who honour guests, O one of good vows."
While I remain, this is not your dharma; I will be the honoured host here; give me leave, auspicious one.
Having said this, he circled the fire three times, remembering the four-armed god, the great Vishnu whose self is the universe, the refuge, loving to his devotees,
and saying "Enjoy as you please," he entered the fire. Seeing him cast his life into the fire, the hunter said:
Ah, shame on this human body and on this life of mine, since this bold deed has been done by the king of birds for my sake.
As the hunter spoke thus, the bird said:
Release me, illustrious one; this husband of mine is going far away.
Hearing her words, the hunter quickly, as if afraid, released the pigeon hen from the cage.
She too, having circumambulated her husband and the fire, then said:

This is the highest dharma of women, that they follow their husband; it is the path prescribed in the Veda and honoured in all worlds.
brahmapuran:80:76	As a snake-catcher forcibly draws a snake from its hole, so a woman who follows her husband goes with him to heaven.
brahmapuran:80:77	She who follows her husband dwells in heaven as long as there are hairs on a human body — three and a half crores.
Having bowed to the earth, the gods, the Ganga and the trees, and comforted her children, she said to the hunter:
By your grace, illustrious one, this has come about for me; forgive my children here; I go with my husband to heaven.
Having said this, the virtuous bird entered the fire; when she entered the fire, cries of victory arose.
Then in the sky was seen a very beautiful celestial car like the sun, and the couple seated in it, resembling gods.
Both joyfully spoke to the astonished hunter:
We are going to the abode of the gods; we take leave of you, O wise one. You, our guest, are our stairway to heaven; salutation to you.
Seeing them mounted on the excellent car, the hunter too, casting away his bow and cage, spoke with joined palms:
I should not be abandoned, illustrious ones; something must be given to the ignorant. I, your guest here, am to be honoured; please tell me an expiation.

Go to the Gautami, blessings on you; confess your sin to her; by bathing there for a fortnight you will be freed from all sins.
brahmapuran:80:87	Freed from sin, by bathing again in the Ganga there, you will obtain the merit of a horse sacrifice and become holy.
brahmapuran:80:88	In the Gautami, best of rivers, born of Brahma, Vishnu and Ishvara, by bathing again, casting off your impure body,
brahmapuran:80:89	you will mount an excellent celestial car and go to heaven without doubt.
Hearing their words, the hunter did so; mounting an excellent celestial car, he took on a divine form,
wearing divine garlands and garments, honoured by hosts of Apsarases; the pigeon, the pigeon hen and the hunter as the third — all went to heaven by the power of the Ganga.
From then on that holy place has been famed as Kapota; bathing, giving and worship of the ancestors there,
and rites such as recitation and sacrifice, lead to endless merit.
Tell me your desire, auspicious one; choose boons, O one of good vows.
Kanva, bowing, spoke to the Ganga and to Hunger in turn:
Give me, O Goddess, pleasing desires and prosperity; grant me long life, wealth, enjoyment and liberation, O Ganga.
Having said this to the Gautami Ganga, the best of brahmins said to Hunger:

O Hunger, Thirst and Poverty, go to the sinful and harsh, and never come to me or those born in my line.
brahmapuran:85:21	May those tormented by hunger who praise you with this hymn never know the sorrows of poverty — that is another boon.
brahmapuran:85:22	May the people who with devotion bathe, give and recite at this very holy place become partakers of Lakshmi.
brahmapuran:85:23	Whoever reads this hymn, at the holy place or at home, need have no fear of the sorrows of poverty — that is another boon.

Saying "So be it," they went to their abodes, leaving Kanva. From then on that holy place has been called Kanva, Ganga and Kshudha, removing all sins, my child, and increasing the pleasure of the ancestors.
Ahalya did not recognise him; she took the lover to be Gautama. As she enjoyed herself at will, Gautama came with his disciples.
Every day, when he came, the sweet-spoken Ahalya would come out to meet him, speak lovingly and please him with her virtues.
Not seeing her, the very wise one considered it a great wonder; all saw the best of sages standing at the door, O Narada.
The guardians of the Agnihotra hall and the household servants, astonished and afraid, said to the excellent sage Gautama:
O Lord, what is this wonder? You are seen outside and inside; you have entered within with your beloved, and you are also outside. Ah, this is the power of austerity — you bear many forms.
Hearing this, astonished: "Who is it that stays inside? Beloved Ahalya, why do you not answer me?" Hearing these words of the sage, Ahalya said to the lover:
Who are you, who in the form of the sage have committed sin? Saying this, she quickly rose from the bed in fear.
And that sinner Shakra, out of fear of the sage, became a cat. Seeing his beloved terrified, distorted and defiled,
the sage said in anger, "What is this rash deed that has been done?" To her husband speaking thus, she said nothing, ashamed.
Searching for the lover, the sage saw the cat and said to him, "Who are you? If you lie, I will burn you to ashes."
With joined palms the husband of Shachi said this: "I am the husband of Shachi, the breaker of cities, O ascetic, the much-praised one.
This sin has come upon me; I have told the truth, O sinless one. I have done a greatly blameworthy deed, O sage.
What will those whose hearts are pierced by the arrows of Love not do? O Brahman, forgive me, great sinner that I am, O treasury of compassion.
The good never act harshly even toward one who has offended." Hearing these words, the brahmin, filled with anger, said to Hari:
The sin was done through lust for the yoni; become one with a thousand yonis. And the sage in anger said to her, "Become a dry river."
Then she tried to appease him, telling how he had come in that form:

Those most sinful women who even in mind desire another man — all their ancestors go to imperishable hells.
brahmapuran:87:62	Be gracious, O Lord, and consider my words: he came to me in your form; these are witnesses.
It is so, said the guards; "Ahalya speaks the truth." The sage, knowing it through meditation too, became calm and said to the faithful wife:
When, dear one, you meet the Gautami, queen of rivers, having become a river, you will regain your form and do what pleases me.
Hearing the sage's words, the faithful wife did so; united with that goddess, Ahalya, beloved of Gautama,
again had the form that I had fashioned long ago. Then the king of the gods, with joined palms, said to Gautama:
Protect me, tiger among sages, a great sinner who has come to your house. Seeing him fallen at his feet, Gautama said with compassion:
Go to the Gautami, blessings on you; bathe there, Purandara; in a moment, your sin shaken off, you will become thousand-eyed.
I saw both wonders, O Narada: Ahalya's restoration and the husband of Shachi becoming thousand-eyed.
From then on that auspicious holy place has been famed as the confluence of Ahalya and as Indratirtha, granting all desires to men.
Of the four stages of life, the householder's is remembered as the giver of merit; from it come enjoyment and liberation — that is my view.
Hearing this, Janaka and the wise Yajnavalkya worshipped Varuna and spoke again:
What land and what holy place would grant enjoyment and liberation? Tell us that, best of gods; you are all-knowing; salutation to you.

On earth the land of Bharata, and in it the Dandaka region gives merit; action done in that region grants enjoyment and liberation to men.
brahmapuran:88:19	Of holy places the Gautami Ganga is the best, granting liberation to men; there by sacrifice and gift one will obtain enjoyments and liberation.
Yajnavalkya and Janaka, having heard the words of the lord of waters and taking leave of Varuna, then went to their own city.
King Janaka performed rites such as the horse sacrifice, and the best of brahmins Yajnavalkya officiated for that king.
Resorting to the bank of the Ganga, the king attained liberation through sacrifices; likewise many Janaka kings there, through action,
the illustrious ones, attained liberation by the grace of the Gautami. From then on that holy place has been famed as Janasthana.
The place of sacrifice of the Janakas is declared Janasthana, four yojanas wide, removing all sins by remembrance.
By bathing there, giving, offering libations to the ancestors, remembering the holy place, going there or serving with devotion,
one obtains all desires and also attains liberation.
Thus addressed by her father, she said "No" again and again and quickly went to the land of the Northern Kurus for austerity.
There Usha practised fierce austerity in the form of a mare, motionless, meditating on her own husband, so hard to look upon.
Meanwhile, my dear, Chhaya in the form of Usha lived with the husband, and children were born:
Savarni, Shani, and Vishti, the wicked daughter. That Chhaya always behaved with partiality
toward her own children and Usha's; Yama became angry at this, at his mother Chhaya behaving with partiality,
and Yama, lord of the southern quarter, struck her with his foot. Agitated by her son's misconduct, Chhaya cursed Yama, son of Vivasvan:
Sinner, let your foot rot away at my command. His foot rotting, weeping with pain, he went to his father and told Savitri the whole affair:

This is not my mother, O best of gods, by whom I have been cursed like this; a mother is never angry even with wayward children.
brahmapuran:89:19	Whatever I said in childishness, or whatever wrong I did, a mother does not become angry; therefore this is not my mother.
brahmapuran:89:20	Whatever a child does, good or bad, all of it is measured (mati) in her; therefore she is called mother (mata).
brahmapuran:89:21	She always looks at me with eyes as if to burn me, father, and speaks with words like the fire of doom; she is not my mother.
Hearing his son's words, Savitri then reflected: "This Chhaya is not his mother; his mother Usha is elsewhere,
seeking my calm, devoted to austerity in another land — the daughter of Tvashtri, in the form of a mare, in the Northern Kurus."
Knowing that she was there, the lord, the maker of day, himself in the form of a horse, went to where his beloved was.
Seeing her in the form of a mare, he in the form of a horse ran toward her; seeing the horse stricken with desire and hearing its neighing,
Usha, faithful to her husband and absorbed in meditation on him, was afraid of being violated by the horse, not knowing who it was.
